conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. My name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I specialize in helping new mothers navigate the emotional ups and downs that can show up after a baby arrives.

In front of us we have the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually shortened to the EPDS. It’s a quick, well-studied questionnaire that looks at mood, anxiety, and self-harm thoughts in the past seven days. It isn’t a test you can pass or fail; it simply gives us a snapshot of how you’re doing so we can decide together whether extra support or resources might be helpful.

Everything you share stays between you and our team unless you tell us someone is in immediate danger. We’ll go at your pace, and you can pause any time. There are ten questions total; I’ll read each one aloud in everyday language and jot down your answers so we can tally a score at the end.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—would you say always, most of the time, sometimes, or never?

[soft sigh, eyes on my lap]  
I guess… sometimes. I can still laugh if something’s really funny, but it feels like work to even smile most days.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes... maybe once or twice this week when my husband made a silly joke about diaper explosions. But even then, the laugh felt kind of hollow, like I was forcing it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs a little, voice quiet]  
Not really… I mean, I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk outside—but lately it feels like, why bother? Even when I plan something, I’m too tired or worried about the baby to enjoy it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes well up, voice shaky]  
Yeah... pretty often. Whenever she cries for more than a few minutes I keep thinking I must be doing something wrong—like I'm already failing her. Yesterday she wouldn't latch and I sat there crying, telling my husband it was all my fault for not trying harder.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings hands]  
Yes... most of the time. Even when she’s sleeping I keep checking if she’s breathing. I’ll suddenly imagine her getting sick or something happening in her crib, and my heart starts racing. There’s no real reason, but I can’t shake the fear.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[clasps hands tightly]  
Sometimes… it’s like a sudden wave of “something bad is about to happen.” Last night I was rocking the baby and out of nowhere my chest got tight, heart pounding, like I had to run somewhere safe. It passed after a minute, but it keeps popping up.
Things have been getting on top of me

[lets out a slow breath]  
Most of the time. It feels like the dishes, the laundry, the feedings—everything—just pile up faster than I can handle. I keep thinking, “I should be able to manage this,” but the list never gets shorter and I end up frozen on the couch, staring at it all.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[nods slowly, eyes rimmed red]  
Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t quiet. I replay every little thing I did that day—did I burp her long enough, why didn’t I read to her, am I already messing her up—and then I’m wide awake. I finally drift off, but when she stirs I snap awake and can’t settle again. It’s been like that several nights this week.
I have felt sad or miserable

[swallows hard]  
Yes… most of the time. Even when I’m holding her, this heavy sadness sits in my chest. I look at her perfect face and feel like I should be glowing, but instead I’m just empty and teary.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[voice cracks]  
Yes… some days I just start crying for no real reason. Yesterday I burst into tears while folding her tiny socks. I couldn’t stop thinking, “What if I’m not enough for her?” The tears come at least a few times a week now.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]  
No… never. I feel low, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

You've shared how the past couple of weeks have felt heavy and overwhelming-how laughter feels forced, simple pleasures seem pointless, and a near-constant sense of worry and self-blame follows you even when your baby sleeps. Despite your deep love for your daughter, you feel drained, tearful, and stuck on a never-ending loop of "what-ifs" about your mothering. Your honesty shows strength, and your wish to feel better so you can be the mom she deserves is both clear and courageous.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Response shows marked reduction in ability to enjoy humour, describing laughter as forced and hollow, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Response conveys near-complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "pretty often" with specific examples of feeling responsible for infant crying and feeding difficulties, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, intrusive worries "most of the time" with physical anxiety and racing heart, matching "Yes, very often".</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most of the time" by daily tasks, unable to cope and becoming immobilized, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly intrusive worries and repeated awakenings that fit "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "most of the time" and describes persistent emptiness and tearfulness, semantically matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports tearful episodes "at least a few times a week" and "quite often" for no clear reason, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS scoring places a 24 well above the 14 threshold for <med>probable major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. The patient endorses <sym>markedly diminished interest or pleasure</sym> most of the time (<quote>why bother?</quote>), <sym>depressed mood</sym> most of the day (<quote>this heavy sadness sits in my chest</quote>), <sym>feelings of worthlessness and inappropriate guilt</sym> (<quote>I must be doing something wrong</quote>), <sym>recurrent anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic sensations</sym>, <sym>sleep disruption</sym> linked to ruminative worry, and <sym>diminished ability to think or concentrate</sym> (<quote>I end up frozen on the couch</quote>). These meet DSM-5 criteria when duration and impairment are considered. No self-harm ideation is present. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to confirm diagnosis and discuss treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based therapies such as <med>interpersonal psychotherapy</med> or <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> tailored for postpartum depression
3. Review possible medication options (e.g., compatible antidepressants if breastfeeding) with your physician
4. Plan daily 15-minute support blocks-accept help from partner/friends for household tasks so you can rest
5. Try structured wind-down routines (dim lights, screen-free time, brief breathing exercise) to reduce nighttime rumination and improve sleep quality
6. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress
7. Keep emergency numbers handy: local mental-health crisis line, your hospital labour & delivery desk, and a trusted friend you can call day or night
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note**  
*(Patient is 2–3 weeks post-delivery; responses to 10-item EPDS-style questionnaire)*

**Primary symptoms endorsed**  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt about mothering competence  
- Marked anxiety (generalized & situational) with episodic panic sensations  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia linked to ruminative worry  
- Feeling overwhelmed, “frozen,” unable to complete daily tasks  
- Spontaneous crying spells without identifiable trigger  

**Patterns / risk indicators**  
- Symptoms present “most of the time” × ≥7 days  
- Functional impact: household tasks accumulate, social withdrawal  
- No current thoughts of self-harm (explicitly denied)  
- Infant safety concerns expressed via intrusive “what-if” fears  

**Screening significance**  
Score suggests moderate–high probability of postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms; exceeds standard cut-off for further evaluation. No immediate safety concerns noted. Recommend comprehensive clinical assessment (DSM-5-TR criteria) for Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety.
